s.d: $ax^2+bx+c=0 \Rightarrow x^2+\frac bax=-\frac ca \Rightarrow \left(x+\frac b{2a}\right)^2=\frac{b^2-4ac}{4a^2}$; take square roots.

s.f: D>0:\ \text{real, distinct};\quad D=0:\ \text{real, equal}\ \left(-\tfrac b{2a}\right);\quad D<0:\ \text{complex conjugates}
s.n: If $a,b,c\in\mathbb Q$ and $D$ is a perfect square, roots are rational. Irrational roots of a rational quadratic come in pairs $p\pm\sqrt q$.

s.q: Roots in terms of each other: $\alpha=k\beta$
One root is the square of the other
Equal and opposite roots / reciprocal roots
Sum of reciprocals and squares of reciprocals

s.f: \text{integer roots}\Rightarrow D\ \text{perfect square and } -b\pm\sqrt D\ \text{divisible by } 2a

s.q: Root of $f(x)=0$ lies in an interval if values differ in sign
s.f: f(p)f(q)<0\Rightarrow\text{an odd number of roots in }(p,q)

s.d: Cross-multiplication: $\frac{\alpha^2}{b_1c_2-b_2c_1}=\frac{\alpha}{c_1a_2-c_2a_1}=\frac1{a_1b_2-a_2b_1}$; square the middle ratio and equate.

s: Graph and sign of the quadratic

s.n: Minimum value $-\frac D{4a}$ if $a>0$; maximum if $a<0$.

s.f: ax^2+bx+c>0\ \forall x\iff a>0,\ D<0;\qquad <0\ \forall x\iff a<0,\ D<0

s.q: Range of quadratic on an interval
s.f: \text{check } f(p),\ f(q)\ \text{and } f\!\left(-\tfrac b{2a}\right)\text{ if } -\tfrac b{2a}\in[p,q]
a>0:\ \text{opens up};\ D>0\ \text{cuts }x\text{-axis twice},\ D=0\ \text{touches},\ D<0\ \text{above axis}

s.q: Maximum and minimum of $ax^2+bx+c$ with $x$ restricted
s.f: x\in[p,q]:\ \text{extremes at } p,\ q\ \text{or the vertex}
\text{put } t=\sin x\ (t\in[-1,1]),\ t=e^x\ (t>0),\ \text{solve with the restricted range}

s.q: Both roots of different quadratics interlace
s.f: \text{roots of } f \text{ separate those of } g\iff f(\alpha_g)f(\beta_g)<0
\#\text{positive roots}\le\text{sign changes in } f(x);\qquad \#\text{negative roots}\le\text{sign changes in } f(-x)
s.n: The difference is an even number.

s.f: \alpha\ \text{is a root of multiplicity } r \iff f(\alpha)=f'(\alpha)=\cdots=f^{(r-1)}(\alpha)=0,\ f^{(r)}(\alpha)\ne0

s.q: Sum of cubes of cubic roots
Roots in AP / GP for a cubic
s.f: \text{AP: take } a-d,a,a+d\ (\text{so } a=-\tfrac b{3a_0});\qquad\text{GP: take } \tfrac ar,a,ar\ (a^3=-\tfrac d{a_0})

s.q: Number of real roots of a polynomial via derivative
s.f: \text{between two roots of } f \text{ lies a root of } f'\ (\text{Rolle})

s.q: Complex roots of a real polynomial
s.f: \text{come in conjugate pairs};\ \text{an odd-degree real polynomial has a real root}
x^2-a|x|+b=0:\ \text{solve } t^2-at+b=0,\ t=|x|\ge0;\ \text{each positive } t \text{ gives two } x

s.q: Condition for $ax^2+2hxy+by^2+2gx+2fy+c$ to factor into two linear factors

s.f: \text{cross-multiply to a quadratic in } x;\ \text{require } D\ge0\ \text{for real } x

s.q: Maximum/minimum of a rational expression in $x$

s: If this type comes, solve like this

s.q: If the question gives $\alpha^n+\beta^n$ (called $P_n$, $S_n$ or $a_n$) and asks for a ratio or combination of very high powers
s.r: You see $P_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n$ (or $\alpha^n-\beta^n$) with big indices like $P_{10}, P_{17}, a_{2024}$, and an expression such as $\frac{P_{17}P_{20}+kP_{17}P_{19}}{\ldots}$.
s.s: Write the quadratic whose roots are $\alpha,\beta$. || Multiply $a\alpha^2+b\alpha+c=0$ by $\alpha^n$ and the same for $\beta$; adding gives the recurrence $aS_{n+2}+bS_{n+1}+cS_n=0$. || Look at the asked expression: group terms so they look like $aS_{n+2}+bS_{n+1}$ — that equals $-cS_n$. || Everything collapses to a simple multiple of one $S_k$; cancel and finish.
s.n: If $P_{10},P_9,P_8$ are given numerically, the recurrence $P_{10}=pP_9+qP_8$ tells you $p,q$, i.e. the quadratic itself.
s.h: Trap: do not try to expand $\alpha^{20}$; and for $\alpha^n-\beta^n$ the same recurrence still holds.

s.q: If it asks you to form a new quadratic whose roots are some function of $\alpha$ and $\beta$
s.r: "Find the equation whose roots are $\frac1\alpha,\frac1\beta$" or "$\alpha^4+\beta^4$ and $\frac{1}{10}(\alpha^6+\beta^6)$" or "$\frac{3\alpha}{\beta}$ and $\frac{4\alpha}{\gamma}$".
s.f: x^2-(\text{sum of new roots})\,x+(\text{product of new roots})=0
s.s: From the given equation write $\alpha+\beta=-\frac ba$ and $\alpha\beta=\frac ca$. || Express the sum and the product of the new roots in terms of $\alpha+\beta$ and $\alpha\beta$ (use $\alpha^2+\beta^2=(\alpha+\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta$ etc.). || Write $x^2-(\text{sum})x+\text{product}=0$. || Shortcut for simple maps: roots $\frac1\alpha$ → replace $x$ by $\frac1x$; roots $k\alpha$ → replace $x$ by $\frac xk$; roots $\alpha+k$ → replace $x$ by $x-k$.
s.e: $x^2-3x+2=0$ has roots $1,2$. Roots doubled: replace $x\to\frac x2$: $\frac{x^2}4-\frac{3x}2+2=0\Rightarrow x^2-6x+8=0$ (roots $2,4$ ✓).

s.q: If the roots must lie in an interval, both be greater/less than a number, or have the same sign
s.r: Phrases like "both roots lie in $[1,5]$", "one root in $(0,2)$ and the other in $(2,3)$", "both roots positive", "$k$ lies between the roots".
s.s: Sketch the parabola $y=f(x)$ (opening up if $a>0$). || Both roots in $(p,q)$: $D\ge0$, $af(p)>0$, $af(q)>0$, $p<-\frac b{2a}<q$. || One root in $(p,q)$ only: $f(p)\,f(q)<0$. || $k$ between the roots: $af(k)<0$ (no need to check $D$). || Both positive: $D\ge0$, sum $>0$, product $>0$. || Intersect all conditions and count the allowed parameter values.
s.h: Trap: if the leading coefficient contains the parameter, multiply by $a$ (use $af(k)$), and check the case $a=0$ separately.

s.q: If two quadratics have a common root
s.r: Two equations are given, with sentences like "$\alpha,\beta$ are roots of the first and $\alpha,\gamma$ are roots of the second".
s.f: \text{Common root: subtract the equations (after equalising the } x^2 \text{ coefficients)}
s.s: Make the $x^2$ coefficients equal and subtract: the $x^2$ terms cancel, giving a linear equation that gives the common root $\alpha$. || Put $\alpha$ back in one equation to get the parameter. || Use sum/product of roots in each equation to get the other roots $\beta$, $\gamma$. || Answer the asked combination.
s.e: $x^2-x+2\lambda=0$ and $3x^2-10x+27\lambda=0$ share $\alpha$. $3\times$first − second: $7x-21\lambda=0\Rightarrow\alpha=3\lambda$; put in the first: $9\lambda^2-3\lambda+2\lambda=0\Rightarrow\lambda=\frac19$.
s.h: Trap: "both roots common" means the coefficients are proportional — a different condition.

s.q: If the equation is in $e^x$, $a^x$, $(\sqrt3+\sqrt2)^x$, $9^{\tan^2x}$ etc. and asks for the number or sum of real solutions
s.r: Exponentials with the same base appear in powers like $e^{4x},e^{3x},e^{2x},e^x$, or pairs whose product is $1$ like $(\sqrt3+\sqrt2)^x$ and $(\sqrt3-\sqrt2)^x$.
s.s: Substitute $t=a^x$ (always $t>0$). || If the polynomial in $t$ is palindromic (coefficients read the same both ways), divide by $t^2$ and put $u=t+\frac1t$ ($u\ge2$ for $t>0$). || Solve for $u$, then $t$; keep only positive $t$. || Each valid $t$ gives exactly one $x=\ln t$; count them (or add the $x$'s: $x_1+x_2=\ln(t_1t_2)$).
s.h: Trap: when the exponent is $x^2-4$ instead of $x$, each value of the exponent gives two values of $x$.

s.q: If a quadratic expression with a parameter must be always positive, or must have real/equal roots
s.r: "is positive for all $x\in\mathbb R$", "has equal roots", "has real roots", with the parameter inside the coefficients.
s.f: ax^2+bx+c>0\ \forall x\iff a>0,\ D<0;\qquad\text{equal roots}\iff D=0
s.s: Identify $a,b,c$ in terms of the parameter. || Write the needed conditions on $a$ and $D$. || Solve the inequalities and intersect. || Count integer values if asked; check $a=0$ separately (then it is linear).
s.n: For $a(b-c)x^2+b(c-a)x+c(a-b)=0$, $x=1$ is always a root (coefficients add to 0). Equal roots then means both roots are 1.

s.q: If it asks the range of $y=\frac{a_1x^2+b_1x+c_1}{a_2x^2+b_2x+c_2}$
s.r: A function defined as a ratio of two quadratics, and "range of $f$ is…".
s.s: Put $y=f(x)$ and cross-multiply. || Collect as a quadratic in $x$: $(a_2y-a_1)x^2+(b_2y-b_1)x+(c_2y-c_1)=0$. || For real $x$ need discriminant $\ge0$; solve this inequality in $y$. || Check $y$ values that would need an excluded $x$ (zeros of the denominator) and the case where the $x^2$ coefficient vanishes.

s.q: If the roots must be integers or rational numbers
s.r: "integral roots", "rational roots", "$\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb N$", or "if $2-\sqrt3$ is a root and $p,q\in\mathbb Q$".
s.f: \text{rational roots}\iff D\ \text{is a perfect square};\quad\text{irrational roots come in pairs } p\pm\sqrt q
s.s: For integer/rational roots, write $D$ and demand it be a perfect square; list the possibilities. || For a root like $2-\sqrt3$ with rational coefficients, the other root is $2+\sqrt3$; use sum and product. || For natural-number roots with a given sum, list factor pairs of the product.
s.e: $x^2+4x-n=0$ has integer roots iff $16+4n$ is a perfect square, i.e. $n+4$ is a perfect square.

s.q: If it asks a symmetric value like $a^4+b^4+c^4$ from $a+b+c$, $ab+bc+ca$, $abc$ (cubic roots)
s.r: Three numbers (or three roots of a cubic) and the values of their elementary sums are given.
s.s: Write $e_1=a+b+c$, $e_2=ab+bc+ca$, $e_3=abc$. || Compute $p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4$ (power sums) one after the other with Newton's identities. || Substitute the numbers.

s.q: If a log, surd or modulus equation turns into a quadratic
s.r: Logs with swapped bases ($\log_{(x+1)}\ldots$ and $\log_{(2x+5)}\ldots$), or $\sqrt x$ with $x$, or $|\sqrt x-3|$.
s.s: Factor the log arguments so the same two bases appear. || Put $t=\log_ab$; the other log becomes $\frac1t$; solve the quadratic in $t$. || For surds, put $t=\sqrt x\ge0$. || Check the domain at the end.

s.q: If the value of an infinite continued fraction is asked
s.s: Call the whole value $y$. || After one full period ($a$, then $b$) the pattern repeats, so the tail equals $y$. || Simplify to a quadratic in $y$ and take the positive root.

s.q: Less common forms (shifted sums, root maps, polynomial composition)
s.r: Equations built from sums like $x(x+2)+(x+1)(x+3)+\cdots$, or "whenever $\alpha$ is a root so is $\alpha^2-2$", or $(x^2-9x+11)^2-(x-4)(x-5)=3$.
s.f: \text{use } \sum k,\ \sum k^2;\ \ \text{substitute a common block } u
s.s: Expand sums using $\sum k=\frac{n(n+1)}2$ and $\sum k^2$ to get an ordinary quadratic. || For root maps, roots must be fixed points of the map or form a 2-cycle; list the cases. || For composite forms, put $u=$ the repeated block and solve in $u$ first.
